The new page had more signups because it also had more visitors. The old page converted 100 of 1,000 visitors, or 10%; the new page converted 160 of 2,000, or 8%.

So the new page’s observed conversion rate was lower, despite its higher signup count. These are descriptive results, and no significance analysis has been done, so they don’t establish that either page converts better.

A database index works like the index at the back of a book. Instead of reading every page to find a topic, you look it up in the index and jump to the right pages. Similarly, a database can use an index to find matching rows without checking the entire table.

For example, an index on customer email addresses can help a database find a customer’s record when you search by email.

The tradeoff is that indexes take up storage and need maintenance. When relevant data is inserted, updated, or deleted, the database must update the index too, adding work to those writes. Not every query benefits: an email index may not help a search by shipping city.

Daily and weekly totals count visitors differently. The daily view counts each person once per day; the weekly view counts them once for the whole week. Someone who visits Monday and Tuesday adds one to each day’s total but only one to the weekly total.

This is expected, not a reporting error. We should label the views “daily unique visitors” and “weekly unique visitors” to make the difference clear.

We can’t yet say whether the reminder emails reduced missed appointments. The missed-appointment rate fell from 18% in August to 12% in September, when the emails began. But September also had a different mix of appointment types and a new cancellation policy, and there was no randomized comparison.

The data shows an association, not a demonstrated causal effect. The next useful check is to compare like-for-like appointment types and, if feasible, test reminders using randomized assignment to better isolate their effect.
